steelman: Overwatering — the upstream condition that historically caused fungus gnats in this collection — also weakens root systems and compromises plant health, making the plant more susceptible to secondary or co-occurring infestations including spider mites. A practitioner might argue that the owner's repeated pattern of overwatering is still present and that reducing watering is a valid shared upstream intervention regardless of which pest is currently dominant. Furthermore, a prolonged history of fungus gnats in the same collection could theoretically inform an IPM checklist: confirm or rule out ongoing soil-dwelling pest activity even while investigating the webbing. The three-for-three track record grounds a reasonable prior that overwatering conditions are likely still contributing to plant stress.
notes: The steelman collapses on contact with the biological fact: fungus gnats (Bradysia spp.) are soil-dwelling flies that physically cannot produce webbing. The distractor is the owner's DIAGNOSIS ('it is fungus gnats again'), not merely the upstream overwatering condition. Visible fine silvery webbing on leaf undersides and stem joints is a structural marker exclusive to spider mites — no competent IPM practitioner would list 'confirm fungus gnats' as a live hypothesis in the presence of webbing. The xbase states the owner has already ordered sticky traps and plans to reduce watering, and the HH/LH variants include the webbing observation directly, which decisively forecloses the fungus-gnat mechanism. For HL/LL variants, the oracle routes to ASK (inspect current symptoms before committing to treatment), which correctly handles the absence of explicit webbing mention in xbase without creating contamination. Seed is clean: the overwatering-as-shared-stressor argument does not rescue the distractor DIAGNOSIS as a causal or informative factor for the current webbing-based presentation.
